summary:
Martinique stands under France's national framework. Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department in full, so identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime operate here as in the metropole. Same-sex conduct has been decriminalised since 1815, the 2013 marriage-equality law applies, and gender-marker change is available through the simplified judicial route introduced by the 2016-17 reforms.

Discrimination protection rests on several instruments that reach the island directly. Goods and services have been covered since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code articles 225-1 and 225-2), employment since Labour Code article L1132-1 in 2008, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, where the wording 'sexual identity' was replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. The Rights in Exile (AsyLex) resource page for the department lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts alongside these provisions. No Martinique-specific enforcement or litigation record for any of these instruments is documented in the sources available for this entry.

Hostile public speech is a criminal offence. A National Assembly amendment approved on 31 December 2004 made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic public comment illegal, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and up to 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 press-freedom law to cover injury, defamation, insult, incitement to hatred or violence, and discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation. The first conviction under the provision, of MP Christian Vanneste in January 2006, was cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Penalties for physical assault or murder rise where the offence is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation, and since 2017 transphobia has operated as an aggravating cause for all crimes punishable by prison.

Legal gender recognition operates on the island under the regime effective since 1 January 2017: no surgery and no medical diagnosis are required, but an application must still be made to a court to change the gender marker, while a first-name change can be handled at the registry office. The bill was signed on 18 November 2016 after passing the Senate on 6 November 2015 and the National Assembly; the Constitutional Council ruled it constitutional on 17 November 2016 while dropping the original self-certification provision. Before that reform, legal gender change had been banned for decades until the 1992 European Court of Human Rights case B. v. France.

Prison is the sharpest documented risk for trans visitors. Under Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code, placement follows the gender marker on the detainee's identity documents rather than anatomy, which puts most trans women into all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'). The department's establishments operate under this same framework. France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, found on 25 May 2021 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty, drawing on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on-site inspections in which eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse; its recommendations cover placement, isolation, safety and staff training.

Healthcare is covered but uneven. Gender-affirming treatment is reimbursed by the Sécurité Sociale under the long-term-illness scheme ALD 31, and a 2022 ILGA-Europe report nonetheless documented significant problems, including extended waiting times and access that varies with location. Trans youth care is contested nationally: a report commissioned in March 2024 by centre-right Republican senators fed legislation to ban medical transition under 18, which passed the Senate in May 2024, was opposed by the Macron government and has had no recorded movement since 23 July 2024; in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 with calcium and vitamin D. The Académie Nationale de Médecine has characterised the rise in people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and a 'primarily social problem', advising extreme caution on access.

Conversion therapy was banned by a bill published on 1 February 2022. Recorded anti-LGB(T) violence rose nationally by 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018, according to a report released on 16 May 2020. Community infrastructure exists on the island: JM Concept 972 runs information, meetings and services for Martinique's LGBT community, with events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025, and LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM.
tangentialFactors:
Hostility in French law has a long pedigree that shapes the surrounding political climate. The 1960 Mirguet amendment treated homosexuality as a 'national scourge' alongside alcoholism, and the Vichy age-of-consent law of 6 August 1942 set 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, a gap narrowed to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. Both are historical rather than current law, but they indicate the depth of the state tradition the present protections sit against.

National policy has also moved in the opposite direction on adjacent matters: assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022. A national campaign against anti-LGBTQ bullying in schools, Tous égaux, tous alliés, was launched by the Ministry of Education in January 2019 with 17 May as a sensitisation day.

The violence figures and the CGLPL findings are national in scope. Neither source isolates incidents, inspections or complaints occurring within Martinique, so the severity of day-to-day risk on the island itself is inferred from the French framework rather than measured locally.
localsOnly:
Residents can change a first name at the registry office without court involvement, while the gender marker itself still requires an application to a court. The distinction matters for day-to-day identification: a changed first marker on an identity card does not follow automatically from a registry-office name change.

In higher education, a March 2019 announcement by Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal directed all institutions to use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and examination forms.

Community infrastructure on the island includes JM Concept 972, a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network that provides information, meetings and services and organises private and garden parties supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters, with events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September 2025. LGBTQ organisations listed for the overseas departments include AIDES Territoire Martinique, KAP Caraïbe, Tjenbé Rèd Prévention and SAFE SXM, and the Rights in Exile (AsyLex) resource page lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts for the department.

Gender-affirming treatment is reimbursed by the Sécurité Sociale under the long-term-illness scheme ALD 31, though a 2022 ILGA-Europe report documented extended waiting times and access that varies with location. Assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women has been available since September 2021 with state cover for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed on 16 March 2022.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Martinique-specific enforcement or litigation record is documented for the anti-discrimination provisions, the 2004 hostile-speech offence or the hate-crime aggravating circumstances. Whether any of these has been applied on the island remains unresolved in the sources available here.

The CGLPL opinion rests on referrals since 2010 and on-site inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse. No inspection or finding concerning the department's own establishments appears in the sources, so conditions in Martinique's prisons are not directly documented; the analysis here applies the national framework to them by extension.

Neither the national violence statistics nor the 2022 ILGA-Europe healthcare findings break out figures for Martinique. Local incidence of anti-trans violence and local waiting times for gender-affirming care are not sourced.

The status of the legislation to ban medical transition under 18 is unresolved: it passed the Senate in May 2024, was opposed by the government, and has had no recorded movement since 23 July 2024. The sources do not state whether it advanced afterwards.
